title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS2 Mathematics First Term covers, how to study it, and a map of every unit.

p: This term begins with a revision of the SS1 work you need (algebra, fractions, linear equations and angles). Then you learn to write numbers in standard form and to round them, to use logarithms, to work with arithmetic sequences and series, to solve quadratic equations in four ways, to solve simultaneous equations (including a linear and a quadratic equation) and to solve equations by drawing graphs.

Mathematics is learned with a pencil in your hand. Copy each worked example, cover the solution and try it yourself, then check. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Revision: Algebraic Expressions
summary: Terms, like and unlike terms, simplifying, expanding brackets and factorising (common factor, difference of two squares and simple trinomials).

p: In 3x² + 5x − 7 the coefficient of x² is 3, the linear term is 5x and −7 is the constant term. Terms are separated by + or −. Like terms have the same letters with the same powers (3x and 5x; 2y² and −7y²) and can be combined. Unlike terms (3x and 5y; 2x² and 2x) cannot.
Simplify 7x + 3y − 2x + 5y: group the x terms (7x − 2x = 5x) and the y terms (3y + 5y = 8y). Answer: 5x + 8y.

Expanding multiplies every term inside the bracket: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12; −2(3x − 5) = −6x + 10 (negative times negative is positive). Two brackets: (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. (2x − 1)(x + 4) = 2x² + 8x − x − 4 = 2x² + 7x − 4.

Common factor: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3); 4x² + 8x = 4x(x + 2). Difference of two squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), so x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3); 4x² − 25 = (2x + 5)(2x − 5). Simple trinomials: find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle coefficient: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) because 2 × 3 = 6 and 2 + 3 = 5. Always check by expanding.

title: Revision: Fractions, Decimals, Percentages and Linear Equations
summary: Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, adding, multiplying and dividing fractions, and solving linear equations.

p: Fraction to decimal: divide top by bottom (3/4 = 0.75). Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100 (0.75 = 75%). Percentage to fraction: put over 100 and simplify (75% = 75/100 = 3/4). Percentage to decimal: divide by 100.

Add: use a common denominator: 1/4 + 1/3 = 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12. Multiply: top times top, bottom times bottom: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. Divide: keep the first, change to times, flip the second: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.

An equation is like a balance: do the same to both sides. 3x + 5 = 14: subtract 5 to get 3x = 9; divide by 3 to get x = 3. 2x + 3 = 11 gives x = 4. With letters on both sides: 5x − 3 = 2x + 9; collect: 5x − 2x = 9 + 3; 3x = 12; x = 4. With brackets: 3(x + 2) = 18; expand 3x + 6 = 18; 3x = 12; x = 4.
Always check by substituting: for 5x − 7 = 13 with x = 4: 5(4) − 7 = 13 and 20 − 7 = 13, which is correct.

activity: Write 7/8 as a decimal and a percentage (0.875; 87.5%). Work out 3/5 + 1/4 (17/20) and 3/4 ÷ 9/16 (4/3). Solve 4x − 7 = 2x + 9 (x = 8) and 2(x − 3) = 10 (x = 8).

title: Revision: Angles and Geometry
summary: Types of angle, angle facts (straight line, point, vertically opposite), angles in parallel lines and in triangles and polygons.

p: Acute: between 0° and 90°. Right: 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°. Complete turn: 360°.

Complementary angles add up to 90°; supplementary angles add up to 180°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles (where two lines cross) are equal.
With parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles are equal; alternate angles are equal; co-interior (allied) angles add up to 180°.

The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. The interior angles of a polygon with n sides add up to (n − 2) × 180°: a quadrilateral has 360° and a pentagon 540°. The exterior angles of any convex polygon add up to 360°.

activity: Two angles on a straight line are 120° and x. Find x (60°). Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon (720°). A triangle has angles 50° and 65°. Find the third (65°).

title: Numbers: Standard Form
summary: Writing very large and very small numbers as A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10, and multiplying and dividing numbers in standard form.

p: A number is in standard form when it is written as A × 10ⁿ, where A is at least 1 and less than 10, and n is a whole number (an integer). It makes huge and tiny numbers easy to read and compare.

Large number: 5 600 000 = 5.6 × 10⁶ (the decimal point moves 6 places to the left, so the power is positive). 345 000 = 3.45 × 10⁵. Small number: 0.00034 = 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ (the point moves 4 places to the right, so the power is negative). 0.000456 = 4.56 × 10⁻⁴; 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴. Check: 4.56 × 0.0001 = 0.000456.
Multiply: multiply the A parts and add the powers: (2 × 10³) × (3 × 10⁴) = 6 × 10⁷. If A comes out 10 or more, adjust: (6 × 10⁵) × (5 × 10⁴) = 30 × 10⁹ = 3 × 10¹⁰.
Divide: divide the A parts and subtract the powers: (4.5 × 10⁶) ÷ (1.5 × 10³) = 3 × 10³.
Add or subtract: first give both numbers the same power: 3.2 × 10³ + 4.5 × 10² = 3200 + 450 = 3650 = 3.65 × 10³.

title: Numbers: Significant Figures and Percentage Error
summary: Counting and rounding to significant figures and working out percentage error.

p: Rules: non-zero digits are always significant (234 has 3). Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2003 has 4). Leading zeros are not (0.0025 has 2). Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant (2.500 has 4). A number such as 500 is ambiguous (1 or 3 significant figures) unless stated.

Find the required digits, look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up; less than 5 rounds down. 0.035682 to 3 s.f.: digits 3, 5, 6; next is 8, so round up: 0.0357. 3.14159 to 4 s.f.: 3.141 and next is 5, so round up: 3.142. 0.0078234 to 3 s.f.: 7, 8, 2, next is 3, so 0.00782.

Percentage error = (|approximate − exact| ÷ exact) × 100%. A desk measured as 1.23 m but really 1.25 m: error 0.02; 0.02 ÷ 1.25 = 0.016; × 100 = 1.6%. A weight of 48.5 kg read when the true value is 50 kg: 1.5 ÷ 50 = 0.03 = 3%. Using π ≈ 3.14 when π = 3.14159: error 0.00159; 0.00159 ÷ 3.14159 × 100 ≈ 0.05%, a very good approximation.

title: Logarithms: Meaning and Laws
summary: What a logarithm is, common logarithms (base 10), and the product, quotient, power and root laws.

p: A logarithm is the power to which a base must be raised to give a number. If bˣ = y then log_b y = x. Examples: 10² = 100 so log₁₀ 100 = 2; 2³ = 8 so log₂ 8 = 3; 10⁰ = 1 so log 1 = 0. Logarithms to base 10 are called common logarithms and are written log x.

log 1 = 0, log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3, log 10 000 = 4. Each time the number is multiplied by 10 the logarithm goes up by 1. A number between 1 and 10 has a logarithm between 0 and 1; between 10 and 100, between 1 and 2. So log 50 is between 1 and 2 (it is about 1.699).
Product: log(M × N) = log M + log N. Example: log(100 × 1000) = 2 + 3 = 5 (and 100 000 = 10⁵).
Quotient: log(M ÷ N) = log M − log N. Example: log(1000 ÷ 10) = 3 − 1 = 2.
Power: log(Mⁿ) = n log M. Example: log(10³) = 3.
Root: log(ⁿ√M) = (1/n) log M. Example: log(√100) = ½ × 2 = 1.

Special values: log 1 = 0; log 10 = 1; log 10ⁿ = n; log of a base to the same base is 1. In short: multiply means add logs; divide means subtract; power means multiply the log; root means divide the log.

activity: Find log 10 000 (4), log(1/10) (−1), log 5 + log 20 (log 100 = 2) and log 8 in base 2 (3). Is log 50 between 1 and 2? (Yes.)

title: Logarithms: Characteristic, Mantissa and Tables
summary: The two parts of a logarithm, finding logs and antilogs from four-figure tables and bar notation for numbers below 1.

p: log 456 = 2.6590. The whole-number part (2) is the characteristic; the decimal part (0.6590) is the mantissa, which is always positive and comes from the tables.

For a number of 1 or more, characteristic = (number of digits before the decimal point) − 1: 456 gives 2; 4.56 gives 0; 45 600 gives 4. For a number less than 1, characteristic = −(number of zeros after the point + 1), written with a bar: 0.456 gives 1̄; 0.0456 gives 2̄; 0.00456 gives 3̄.

Write the number in standard form. log 456: 456 = 4.56 × 10². Characteristic 2. In the tables, find row 45 and column 6: mantissa 0.6590. So log 456 = 2.6590. For a fourth digit, add the number from the mean difference column. Same digits give the same mantissa: 567, 56.7, 5.67, 0.567 and 0.0567 all have mantissa 0.7536, so their logs are 2.7536, 1.7536, 0.7536, 1̄.7536 and 2̄.7536.

The antilogarithm undoes the logarithm: if log x = y then x = antilog y. Find antilog 2.6590: mantissa 0.6590 gives 4.56 in the antilog table; characteristic 2 means × 10²; so the number is 456. For antilog 2̄.5340: mantissa 0.5340 gives 3.42; 2̄ means × 10⁻²; the number is 0.0342.

activity: Write the characteristic of log 7 (0), log 70 (1), log 7000 (3), log 0.07 (2̄) and log 0.007 (3̄). Given log 3.42 = 0.5340, find log 34.2 (1.5340), log 3420 (3.5340) and antilog 1̄.5340 (0.342).

title: Calculations with Logarithms and Calculators
summary: Using logs to multiply, divide, raise to powers and find roots, and using the log keys of a scientific calculator.

p: Let N be the answer. Take logs of both sides. Use the laws. Look up each log. Add, subtract or multiply. Find the antilogarithm.

Calculators have a [log] key for base-10 logarithms and a [10ˣ] key (often shift + log) for antilogarithms. To find log 456: press log 456 = to see 2.659. To find antilog 2.659: press 10ˣ 2.659 =. Always check that the answer is reasonable (for example log 456 should be between 2 and 3). A calculator's answers are normally given to more figures than tables; round to the number of significant figures asked for. The [EXP] or [×10ˣ] key enters standard form.

activity: Use logarithms (or a calculator) to find 18.4 × 5.2 (95.68), 624 ÷ 13 (48) and 4³ (64). Why must the logs be added when multiplying? (Because log(M × N) = log M + log N.)

title: Sequences: Meaning and Types
summary: What a sequence is, terms and the nth term, and the main kinds of sequence: arithmetic, geometric and others.

p: A sequence is a list of numbers arranged by a rule. Each number is a term: T₁, T₂, T₃... and Tₙ is the nth term. A rule for Tₙ lets us find any term: if Tₙ = 2n + 1, then T₁ = 3, T₂ = 5, T₃ = 7, T₄ = 9.
Arithmetic progression (AP): each term is found by adding the same number (the common difference d): 2, 5, 8, 11 (d = 3); 20, 15, 10, 5 (d = −5).
Geometric progression (GP): each term is found by multiplying by the same number (the common ratio r): 2, 6, 18, 54 (r = 3).
Other sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16 (Tₙ = n²); Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 (each term is the sum of the two before).
For 3, 7, 11, 15, the differences are all 4, so it is an AP with a = 3 and d = 4. For 5, 10, 20, 40, the ratios are all 2, so it is a GP. The next term in 1, 4, 9, 16 is 25, since the terms are n².

activity: Write the first four terms when Tₙ = 3n − 1 (2, 5, 8, 11). Say what type of sequence 2, 6, 18, 54 is (geometric, r = 3). Find the next two terms of 100, 90, 80 (70, 60).

title: Arithmetic Progression: nth Term and Sum
summary: The formulas Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], with worked examples including finding the number of terms.

p: For an AP with first term a and common difference d: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) where l is the last term.
Here a = 3 and d = 4. T₁₀ = 3 + 9 × 4 = 39. S₁₀ = 10/2 × [2 × 3 + 9 × 4] = 5 × 42 = 210. Check with the other form: 5 × (3 + 39) = 210.
If T₅ = 17 and T₉ = 29: a + 4d = 17 and a + 8d = 29. Subtract: 4d = 12, so d = 3, and a = 17 − 12 = 5. The sequence is 5, 8, 11, 14, 17...

title: Arithmetic Progression: Problems
summary: Using AP formulas to solve everyday problems on savings, sums of numbers and finding the first term and common difference.

p: Find the sum of the first 20 positive even numbers. 2, 4, 6, ...: a = 2, d = 2, n = 20. S₂₀ = 20/2 × [2 × 2 + 19 × 2] = 10 × 42 = 420.
The first 10 odd numbers: a = 1, d = 2, n = 10. S₁₀ = 5 × [2 + 18] = 100. (The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².)

A girl saves ₦500 in the first week and then ₦100 more each week than the week before. How much does she save in week 12, and in total over 12 weeks? a = 500, d = 100. T₁₂ = 500 + 11 × 100 = ₦1 600. S₁₂ = 12/2 × [1000 + 11 × 100] = 6 × 2100 = ₦12 600.

The 3rd term of an AP is 11 and the 7th term is 23. a + 2d = 11 and a + 6d = 23. Subtract: 4d = 12, d = 3, a = 5. The 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62, and the sum of the first 20 terms is 10 × (5 + 62) = 670.

activity: A ladder has 15 rungs. The lowest is 60 cm long and each rung is 2 cm shorter than the one below. Find the length of the top rung (60 − 28 = 32 cm) and the total length of wood for all the rungs (15/2 × (60 + 32) = 690 cm).
